# Box Plots {#ggplot2-box-plot}

## Introduction

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this chart

Box plots compress a distribution into median, quartiles and outliers for fast group comparison.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

Hiding sample size misleads; a slim box from n=5 looks as confident as one from n=5000.
:::

In this chapter, we will learn to:

- build box plots
- modify box 
    - color
    - fill
    - alpha
    - line size
    - line type
- modify outlier 
    - color
    - shape 
    - size 
    - alpha

The box plot is a standardized way of displaying the distribution of data. It 
is useful for detecting outliers and for comparing distributions, and it shows
the shape, central tendency and variability of the data.

## Structure

- the body of the boxplot consists of a "box" (hence, the name), which goes from the first quartile (Q1) to the third quartile (Q3)
- within the box, a vertical line is drawn at the Q2, the median of the data set
- two horizontal lines, called whiskers, extend from the front and back of the box 
- the front whisker goes from Q1 to the smallest non-outlier in the data set, and the back whisker goes from Q3 to the largest non-outlier
- if the data set includes one or more outliers, they are plotted separately as points on the chart


```{r box, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
```

## Data

We will use two different data sets in this chapter. Both data sets have returns
for the same five stocks, but in different formats; the long file has four extra
rows.

```{r show, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
daily_returns <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/tickers.csv')
daily_returns
```

## Single Plot

If you are not comparing the distribution of continuous data, you can create a
box plot for a single variable. Map the variable to `y` and add
`geom_boxplot()`. In the example below, we examine the distribution of
stock returns of Apple.

```{r box2, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(daily_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(y = AAPL))
```

:::{.callout-tip}
Older code (including earlier editions of this book) used
`aes(x = factor(1))` as a dummy grouping variable for single boxplots.
That workaround is no longer needed but still renders, so you may
encounter it in the wild.
:::

## Compare Distributions

### Data

For the rest of the chapter, we will use the data set below. Instead of 5 columns,
we have two. One for the stock names and another for returns.

```{r show2, eval=TRUE, message=FALSE}
tidy_returns <- 
  read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rsquaredacademy/datasets/master/tidy_tickers.csv',
  col_types = list(col_factor(levels = c('AAPL', 'AMZN', 'FB', 'GOOG', 'MSFT')), col_double()))
tidy_returns
```

With the data above, let us create a box plot where we compare the distribution
of stock returns of different companies. We map the X axis to the column with
stock names and the Y axis to the column with stock returns. Note that the
column names are wrapped inside `aes()`.

```{r box3, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns))
```

To create a horizontal box plot, we can use `coord_flip()`, which flips the
coordinate axes.

## Horizontal Box Plot

```{r box4, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns)) +
  coord_flip()
```

### Notch

We use notches to compare medians. Use the `notch` argument and set
it to `TRUE`. 

```{r box5, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns),
    notch = TRUE) 
```

### Jitter

Just for comparison, let us plot the returns as points on top of the box plot
using `geom_jitter()`. We modify the color of the points using the `color`
argument and the spread using the `width` argument.

```{r box6, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns, aes(x = stock, y = returns)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, color = 'blue')
```

## Outliers

To highlight extreme observations, we can modify the appearance of outliers 
using the following:

- color
- shape
- size
- alpha

To modify the color of the outliers, use the `outlier.color` argument. Specify
the color using its name or the associated hex code.

```{r box7, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), outlier.color = 'red')
```

We can modify the shape of the outlier using the `outlier.shape` argument.
It takes values between `0` and `25`.

```{r box9, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), outlier.shape = 23) 
```

We can modify the size of the outlier using the `outlier.size` argument. It
takes any value greater than `0`.

```{r box10, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), outlier.size = 3) 
```

You can play around with the transparency of the outlier using the 
`outlier.alpha` argument. It takes values between `0` and `1`.

```{r box11, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), outlier.color = 'blue', outlier.alpha = 0.3) 
```

## Aesthetics

The appearance of the box can be controlled using the following:

- color
- fill
- alpha
- line type
- line width

### Specify Values 

We can modify the background color of the box using the `fill` argument.
Specify the color using its name or the associated hex code.

```{r box12, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), fill = c('blue', 'red', 'green', 'yellow', 'brown')) 
```

To modify the transparency of the background color, use the `alpha` argument. It
takes any value between `0` and `1`.

```{r box14, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), fill = 'blue', alpha = 0.3) 
```

We can modify the color of the border using the `color` argument. Specify the
color using its name or the associated hex code.

```{r box15, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), color = c('blue', 'red', 'green', 'yellow', 'brown')) 
```

We can change the width of the border using the `linewidth` argument. It takes
any value greater than `0`.

```{r box17, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), linewidth = 1.5) 
```

To change the line type of the border, use the `linetype` argument. It takes
any value between `0` and `6`.

```{r box18, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns), linetype = 2) 
```

## Map Variables

Instead of specifying values, we can also map `fill` and `color` to variables.
In the example below, we map `fill` to the variable stock. It assigns
a different color to each stock.

```{r box13, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns, fill = stock)) 
```

Let us map `color` to the variable stock. It will assign a different color
to each box border.

```{r box16, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(tidy_returns) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = stock, y = returns, color = stock)) 
```

## Exercises

2. Draw a single-variable boxplot of `mpg` using modern syntax (no `factor(1)`).
3. Rewrite the grouped plot with a message-first title and no redundant legend.
